How to use this

Every question follows the same order:

  1. Question, with the figure taken straight from the book.
  2. Try it first (yellow). Cover the rest of the question and solve it.
  3. Hint: what's new (orange). Only when the question brings an idea you haven't met earlier in this PDF. If you're stuck, read it and try again.
  4. Solution in compact assignment form: Given → To find → each step with its intermediate values → boxed answer. Copy it into your submission, or compare it line by line with your attempt to find the step that went wrong.
  5. Side note (grey) or book error (red), only when there is something worth knowing.

The tag next to each question number shows how much teaching it carries: teach full explanation · new idea one new thing · practice plain solution.

If you couldn't solve one, just tell me its number. Nothing else needs marking.

A · Superposition theorem

KVL, KCL, Ohm's law (you have these)→Nodal / mesh: all sources at once→Superposition: one source at a time→Thevenin / Norton (next)

Where this sits. You can already solve any circuit with nodal or mesh analysis, taking every source at once. Superposition breaks the same job into smaller circuits, one source at a time, which is often quicker by hand. It is also the reason Thevenin's theorem works, which comes next.

Three terms first.

  • Linear circuit: made of R, L, C, linear dependent sources and independent sources. Doubling every source doubles every current and voltage.
  • Independent source: a fixed voltage or current (a battery, a 2 A source, 10 cos 4t).
  • Dependent source (diamond symbol): its value follows some other voltage or current in the circuit, for example 2Vx.

Statement. In a linear circuit with several independent sources, any current or voltage is the algebraic sum of the values caused by each independent source acting alone.

Switching a source off means setting its value to zero:

Source Switched off it becomes Why
Ideal voltage source short circuit 0 V across it
Ideal current source open circuit 0 A through it
Dependent source never switched off it is not a source on its own; it follows the circuit

Superposition adds currents and voltages only, not power (P goes as I², and (I′ + I″)² ≠ I′² + I″²).

A1 · Problem 5.1Superposition · DC teach
Question

Find the current I in the circuit shown, using the superposition theorem.

Try it first

Cover everything below. Draw two circuits, 1 V alone and 1 A alone, find the current in the 2 Ω in each, and decide each one's sign before adding.

Hint: what's new
  • The whole method: two sources, so solve two small circuits and add.
  • Switching off: the 1 V source becomes a short; the 1 A source becomes an open.
  • Signs: measure each part against the arrow drawn for I. A part flowing the other way is negative.

Given: 1 A source, 1 V source; 1 Ω (series), 1 Ω (shunt), 2 Ω, 3 Ω.

To find: I through the 2 Ω (left → right).

Case (i): 1 V alone (1 A opened). The series 1 Ω carries nothing. The 3 Ω sits directly across the 1 V, so it changes nothing else. The 1 V drives current through 2 Ω + 1 Ω (shunt):

current = 12 + 1 = 13 A (right → left)⇒I′ = −13 A

Case (ii): 1 A alone (1 V shorted, so the 3 Ω is shorted out). The 1 A divides between the 1 Ω shunt and the 2 Ω:

I″ = 1 × 11 + 2 = 13 A (left → right)

Superposition: I = I′ + I″ = −13 + 13 = 0

Answer

I = 0 A (= book)

Why zero, and two shortcuts
  • Node check: 1 = VA1 + VA − 12 gives VA = 1 V, the same as the right-hand node, so no current flows in the 2 Ω.
  • An element in series with an ideal current source never changes any other current (the left 1 Ω here).
  • An element in parallel with an ideal voltage source never changes any other current (the 3 Ω here).
A2 · Problem 5.2Superposition · AC teach
Question

Calculate the voltage V across the resistor R by using the superposition theorem.

Try it first

Which elements drop out in each case? Aim for V′ and V″ in the form something1 + j.

Hint: what's new
  • AC (phasor) circuit. j1 Ω is an inductor, −j5 Ω a capacitor. Superposition is unchanged; the arithmetic uses complex numbers.
  • Complex dividers: the same formulas as for resistors, with Z in place of R.
  • The −j5 + j4 branch is across the 1 V source (5.1's shortcut), so it never matters.

Given: 1 A, 1 V; R = 1 Ω, j1 Ω, −j5 Ω, j4 Ω.

To find: V across R (+ at top).

Case (i): 1 A alone (1 V shorted; this also shorts out the −j5 + j4 branch). R ∥ j1 across the 1 A:

V′ = 1 × 1 × j11 + j1 = j1 + j V

Case (ii): 1 V alone (1 A opened). j1 and R in series across 1 V:

I″ = 11 + j⇒V″ = 1 × I″ = 11 + j V

Superposition: V = j1 + j + 11 + j = 1 V

Answer

V = 1∠0° V (= book)

Check

Node equation at the top node: 1 = V1 + V − 1j1 gives V(1 + j) = 1 + j, so V = 1 V ✓.

A3 · Problem 5.3Superposition · dependent source teach
Question

Use the superposition theorem on the circuit shown to find I.

Try it first

Write Vx′ in terms of the loop current in case (i). For case (ii), write one KCL at the top of the 2 Ω and one KVL around the left loop. Expect elevenths.

Hint: what's new
  • Dependent source: it stays in every case. Only the 10 V and the 2 A take turns.
  • Its value changes per case: 2Vx′ in case (i), 2Vx″ in case (ii). Re-find Vx in each sub-circuit.
  • Polarity of Vx: + is at the bottom of the 2 Ω. Most wrong answers to this question come from this sign.

Given: 10 V, 2 A, 5 Ω, 2 Ω, VCVS 2Vx.

To find: I (out of the 10 V source, through the 5 Ω).

Case (i): 10 V alone. One loop, current i′ clockwise (= direction of I), flowing down the 2 Ω, so Vx′ = −2i′.

10 + 2Vx′ = 5i′ + 2i′⇒10 − 4i′ = 7i′⇒I′ = i′ = 1011 A

Case (ii): 2 A alone. At node X: 2 A splits into ix (down the 2 Ω, so Vx″ = −2ix) and i″ (leftward through the dependent source and 5 Ω).

KCL at X:2 = −Vx″2 + i″…(1)
Left loop:5i″ + 3Vx″ = 0⇒i″ = −35Vx″…(2)

(X sits at −Vx″; the dependent source drops another 2Vx″, so the 5 Ω has −3Vx″ across it.)

(2) in (1):2 = −1110Vx″⇒Vx″ = −2011 V,i″ = 1211 A

i″ runs anticlockwise, against I, so I″ = −12/11 A.

Superposition: I = 1011 − 1211 = −211 A

Answer

I = −2/11 A ≈ −0.182 A (= book). The minus sign means the current actually flows into the + of the 10 V source.

Never switch off a dependent source

Shorting 2Vx as if it were independent gives a wrong answer. It stays in; only its value changes from case to case.

A4 · Problem 5.4Superposition · AC new idea
Question

Determine the current in the capacitor branch by the superposition theorem.

Try it first

Which way does each source see Z1 and Z2: in series, or in parallel?

Hint: what's new
  • Source with an angle: 2∠90° A = j2 A. Convert to rectangular form before multiplying.
  • Polar form with a negative real part: a calculator's tan⁻¹ lands in the wrong quadrant; add 180°.

Given: 4∠0° V, 2∠90° A, Z1 = 3 + j4 Ω, Z2 = 3 − j4 Ω.

To find: I in the capacitor branch (left → right).

Case (i): 4∠0° V alone (current source opened). Z1, Z2 in series:

I′ = 4∠0°(3 + j4) + (3 − j4) = 23∠0° A

Case (ii): 2∠90° A alone (voltage source shorted). Z1 ∥ Z2 across the source:

I″ = j2 × 3 + j46 = −43 + j1 A

Superposition: I = 23 − 43 + j1 = −23 + j1 A

|I| = √((2/3)2 + 1) = 1.20 A,θ = 180° − tan−1(1.5) = 123.7°
Answer

I = 1.2∠123.7° A (= book)

Side note

Z1 + Z2 = 6 Ω is purely real (+j4 and −j4 cancel), which is why both cases are clean. Equal and opposite reactances in series act like a short: series resonance, met later.

A5 · Problem 5.5Superposition · AC, DC + AC teach
Question

Find the current i0 using the superposition theorem, in each of circuits (a), (b) and (c).

Try it first

(a) is quick practice. In (b), stop and ask: what does an inductor look like to the 8 V DC source? In (c), redraw the circuit after switching off each source before you calculate anything.

Hint: what's new
  • (b) Two different frequencies (DC and 10 cos 4t). Each case is solved at its own frequency: at DC (ω = 0), XL = ωL = 0, so the inductor is a short; at ω = 4, it is j4 Ω. The two answers are added in the time domain, never as phasors, because phasors only add when they share one frequency.
  • (c) Redraw after switching off. Once the voltage source is shorted, the 6 Ω and the current source both run to ground and everything becomes parallel.

(a) Given: 5∠0° V, 2∠0° A, 4 Ω, −j2 Ω, j5 Ω. To find: i0 (down the capacitor).

5∠0° alone:i0′ = 54 − j2 = 1 + j0.5 A
2∠0° alone (j5 is in series with the source, so irrelevant):i0″ = 2 × 44 − j2 = 1.6 + j0.8 A
Answer

(a) i0 = 2.6 + j1.3 = 2.91∠26.57° A (= book, 2.9∠26.56° A)

(b) Given: 10 cos 4t V, 8 V DC, 4 Ω, 1 H, 2 Ω. To find: i0(t) (down the inductor).

8 V DC alone (AC source shorted; ω = 0, so the inductor is a short):

i0′ = 82 = 4 A(the 4 Ω has 0 V across it)

10 cos 4t alone (8 V shorted; ω = 4 rad/s, ZL = j4 Ω):

Z = 4 + j4 × 22 + j4 = 5.6 + j0.8 Ω,I = 10∠0°Z = 1.75 − j0.25 A
i0″ = I × 22 + j4 = 0.25 − j0.75 = 0.791∠−71.57° A

Superposition (time domain):

Answer

(b) i0(t) = 4 + 0.791 cos(4t − 71.57°) A

Book error in 5.5(b)

The book treats the inductor as j4 Ω for the DC source too, and then adds the DC and AC results as if both were phasors, printing 2.63∠−63.58° A. Both steps are wrong: at DC an inductor is a short, and quantities at different frequencies cannot be added as phasors. The answer above was confirmed by a node solve of each case.

(c) Given: 10∠30° V, 2∠0° A, 8 Ω, −j2 Ω, j4 Ω, 6 Ω. To find: i0 (down the 8 Ω).

10∠30° V alone (current source opened):

Z = 6 + j4 ∥ (8 − j2) = 6 + (1.882 + j3.529) = 7.882 + j3.529 Ω,I = 10∠30°Z = 1.158∠5.88° A
i0′ = I × j4(8 − j2) + j4 = I × j48 + j2 = 0.562∠81.84° A

2∠0° A alone (voltage source shorted). Z = j4 ∥ 6 = 1.846 + j2.769 Ω:

i0″ = 2 × Z(8 − j2) + Z = j2428 + j22 = 0.674∠51.84° A
i0 = (0.080 + j0.556) + (0.416 + j0.530) = 0.496 + j1.086 A
Answer

(c) i0 = 1.19∠65.45° A

Book error in 5.5(c)

The book prints 0.81∠39.38° A. Two slips: in case (i) it divides the current with (8 − j2)/(8 + j2) instead of j4/(8 + j2) (the current into a branch is set by the other branch's impedance); in case (ii) it expands (8 − j2)(3 + j2) + j12 as 12 + j11 instead of 28 + j22. The answer above was confirmed by a full node solve.

A6 · Problem 5.6Superposition · two frequencies new idea
Question

Find v0 using the superposition theorem.

Try it first

Work out XC and XL separately for ω = 5 and ω = 10 before drawing anything.

Hint: what's new
  • Reactances change with frequency. XC = 1ωC and XL = ωL must be recomputed for each source's own ω.
  • Mixed sin and cos: keep each term in the function it started with (sin for the voltage source, cos for the current source).

Given: 30 sin 5t V with 8 Ω; 0.2 F, 1 H, 20 cos 10t A. To find: v0(t).

30 sin 5t alone (ω = 5; current source opened): XC = 15 × 0.2 = 1 Ω → −j1 Ω; XL = 5 × 1 = 5 Ω → j5 Ω.

30 − v′8 = v′−j1 + v′j5⇒v′ = 308(0.125 + j0.8) = 4.631∠−81.12° V

20 cos 10t alone (ω = 10; voltage source shorted): XC = 110 × 0.2 = 0.5 Ω → −j0.5 Ω; XL = 10 Ω → j10 Ω.

20 = v″(18 + 1−j0.5 + 1j10) = v″(0.125 + j1.9)⇒v″ = 10.50∠−86.24° V
Answer

v0(t) = 4.631 sin(5t − 81.12°) + 10.50 cos(10t − 86.24°) V

Book inconsistency in 5.6

The figure gives the current source as 20 cos 10t A, but the book's solution uses 2∠0° A and prints 1.051 cos(10t − 86.24°) for the second term. The answer above follows the figure. If your source is 2 A, the second term is 1.051 cos(10t − 86.24°) V; the first term is unchanged.

A7 · Problem 5.7Superposition · current-controlled source new idea
Question

Find i0 and i from the circuit of the figure using the superposition theorem.

Try it first

In each case, the dependent source's value is 2 × (that case's i0). Write KCL at the middle node and one KVL around the outer loop.

Hint: what's new
  • Controlled by a current, not a voltage (5.3 was voltage-controlled). The rule is the same: keep the source, and re-find its controlling current i0 in each case.

Given: 6 V, 1 A, 1 Ω, 5 Ω, CCVS 2i0. To find: i0, i.

6 V alone (1 A opened): one loop, so i0′ = i′.

6 = 1·i′ + 5·i′ + 2i0′ = 8i′⇒i′ = i0′ = 0.75 A

1 A alone (6 V shorted):

KCL:i″ = 1 + i0″outer KVL:1·i0″ + 5i″ + 2i0″ = 0
⇒3i0″ + 5(1 + i0″) = 0
8i0″ = −5⇒i0″ = −0.625 A,i″ = 0.375 A
Answer

i = 0.75 + 0.375 = 1.125 A, i0 = 0.75 − 0.625 = 0.125 A

Book error in 5.7

The book sets up the same equation, then solves 8i0″ = −5 as i0″ = −5/4 = −1.25 A, and prints i = 0.5 A, i0 = −0.5 A. The correct value is −5/8 = −0.625 A. Direct check: KCL i = i0 + 1 and KVL 6 − i0 − 5i = 2i0 give i0 = 1/8 A ✓.

A8 · Problem 5.8Superposition · AC practice
Question

Using the superposition theorem, calculate the current through the (2 + j3) Ω impedance branch.

Try it first

Series-parallel reduction, twice. Watch which way the branch current flows in case II.

Case I: 30 V alone (20 V shorted). Branch: Zb = (2 + j3) + (6 ∥ 4) = 4.4 + j3 Ω.

Z = 5 + Zb × j5Zb + j5 = 6.32 + j2.60 Ω,I′ = 30Z = 4.06 − j1.67 A,i′ = I′ × j5Zb + j5 = 2.389 + j0.270 A

Case II: 20 V alone (30 V shorted). Branch: Za = (5 ∥ j5) + 2 + j3 = 4.5 + j5.5 Ω.

Z = 4 + 6ZaZa + 6 = 7.31 + j1.41 Ω,I″ = 20Z = 2.638 − j0.509 A
i″ = −I″ × 6Za + 6 = −1.063 + j0.848 A(it flows right → left, against i)
Answer

i = i′ + i″ = 1.326 + j1.117 = 1.73∠40.13° A (= book)

A9 · Problem 5.9Superposition · three sources, open terminals new idea
Question

Using the superposition theorem, find VAB.

Try it first

Three sources, so three cases. Nothing is connected across A–B, so no current leaves at A or B.

Hint: what's new
  • Three sources: same method, one more case.
  • Open terminals: VAB is the voltage across a gap. With no load, the only path is the loop 4 Ω + 2 Ω + 6 Ω, and VAB is the drop across the 6 Ω.
  • Source transformation inside a case: 2 A in parallel with 4 Ω equals an 8 V source in series with 4 Ω, which makes case III a single loop.
Case I (2 V):I′ = 24 + 2 + 6 = 16 A,VAB′ = 6I′ = 1 V
Case II (4 V):I″ = 412 = 13 A,VAB″ = −6I″ = −2 V
Case III (2 A):I‴ = 812 = 23 A,VAB‴ = −6I‴ = −4 V

(In case I the current runs through the 6 Ω from A's side to B's side, so A is higher; in cases II and III it runs the other way, hence the minus signs.)

Answer

VAB = 1 − 2 − 4 = −5 V (= book)

A10 · Problem 5.10Superposition · dependent source, three sources new idea
Question

Find the current i in the circuit shown using the superposition theorem.

Try it first

Case I is one loop. In case II, look for a resistor in series with the dependent source.

Hint: what's new
  • Source transformation works on dependent sources too. In case II, the 4i source in series with the 2 Ω becomes a dependent current source 4i/2 = 2i in parallel with 2 Ω.
  • A current source inside a mesh fixes that mesh current (case III: the 8 A source sets the mesh difference I − 8).

Case I: 10 V alone (2 A and 8 A opened). Loop current i′ clockwise:

−4i′ + 3i′ − 10 + 2i′ = 0⇒i′ = 10 A

Case II: 2 A alone (10 V shorted, 8 A opened). Total (2 + 2i″) splits between 2 Ω and 3 Ω:

i″ = 22 + 3(2 + 2i″)⇒5i″ = 4 + 4i″⇒i″ = 4 A

Case III: 8 A alone (10 V shorted, 2 A opened). Mesh current I; the 3 Ω carries i‴ = I − 8:

−4i‴ + 3(I − 8) + 2I = 0,I = i‴ + 8⇒−4i‴ + 3i‴ + 2i‴ + 16 = 0⇒i‴ = −16 A
Answer

i = 10 + 4 − 16 = −2 A (= book)

A11 · Problem 5.11Superposition · dependent source, three sources practice
Question

Using the superposition theorem, determine V1, the voltage across the 3 Ω resistor.

Try it first

Three cases again; the dependent source 4i stays in all three. Case I has a supermesh around the 8 A source.

Case I: 8 A alone. Supermesh KVL and KCL at node x:

3i′ + 2i1 − 4i′ = 0 ⇒ i1 = i′2;i1 = 8 + i′ ⇒ i′2 = 8 + i′ ⇒ i′ = −16 A,V1′ = 3i′ = −48 V

Case II: 2 A alone. Mesh current i2 on the left; the 3 Ω carries i″ = i2 + 2:

3(i2 + 2) + 2i2 − 4i″ = 0 ⇒ 5i2 + 6 − 4(i2 + 2) = 0 ⇒ i2 = 2 A,i″ = 4 A,V1″ = 12 V

Case III: 10 V alone. One loop:

3i‴ − 10 + 2i‴ − 4i‴ = 0 ⇒ i‴ = 10 A,V1‴ = 30 V
Answer

V1 = −48 + 12 + 30 = −6 V (= book)

A12 · Problem 5.12Superposition · AC new idea
Question

Calculate the current through the impedance (3 + j4) Ω using the superposition theorem.

Try it first

Two voltage sources, same frequency. Get each case's current as a fraction before simplifying.

Hint: what's new
  • The two contributions can cancel. Here they come out equal and opposite, so the branch current is zero. A zero answer is not an error; check it with one node equation.
10∠90° alone:I = j105 + (3 + j4)j53 + j9 = j10(3 + j9)−5 + j60,I′ = I × j53 + j9 = −10−1 + j12 = 0.069 + j0.828 A
10∠0° alone:I = 10j5 + 5(3 + j4)8 + j4 = 10(8 + j4)−5 + j60,I″ = I × 58 + j4 = 10−1 + j12 = −0.069 − j0.828 A
Answer

I = I′ + I″ = 0 A (= book)

Check

Node equation at the top node: V(15 + 13 + j4 + 1j5) = j105 + 10j5 = j2 − j2 = 0, so V = 0 and no current flows in 3 + j4 ✓.

A13 · Problem 5.13Superposition · AC practice
Question

Using the superposition theorem, determine the current in the 4 Ω resistor.

Try it first

Combine the parallel pairs first: 5 Ω ∥ j2 Ω and 2 Ω ∥ −j2 Ω.

Case I: 20∠0° A alone (voltage source shorted). Z1 = 5 ∥ j2 = 0.690 + j1.724 Ω; Z2 = 2 ∥ (−j2) = 1 − j1 Ω.

I1 = 20 × Z1Z1 + 4 + Z2 = 3.145 + j5.660 A(left → right)

Case II: 100∠90° V alone (current source opened). (Z1 + 4) ∥ (−j2) = 0.850 − j1.950 Ω:

Is = j1002 + (0.850 − j1.950) = −16.35 + j23.90 A,VB = Is(0.850 − j1.950) = 32.70 + j52.20 V
I2 = VBZ1 + 4 = 9.748 + j7.547 A(right → left)
Answer

I = I1 − I2 = −6.604 − j1.887 = 6.87∠−164.05° A (left → right), i.e. 6.87 A flowing right → left (= book, 6.89∠−163.67° A, to rounding)

A14 · Problem 5.14Superposition · dependent source practice
Question

Find I in the figure using the superposition theorem.

Try it first

Same idea as 5.3. In case II, the 4 V short joins the two top-left nodes; write one KCL there.

Case I: 4 V alone (2 A opened). One loop; I′ flows up the 2 Ω, so Vx′ = −2I′:

−4 + 3I′ + 5Vx′ − Vx′ = 0 ⇒ 3I′ + 4(−2I′) = 4 ⇒ I′ = −0.8 A

Case II: 2 A alone (4 V shorted). KCL at the top node (voltage Vx″):

2 = Vx″2 + Vx″ − 5Vx″3 ⇒ Vx″ = −2.4 V,I″ = Vx″ − 5Vx″3 = 3.2 A
Answer

I = −0.8 + 3.2 = 2.4 A (= book)

B · Thevenin's and Norton's theorems

Superposition: one source at a time (done)→Thevenin: whole network → one source + one impedance→Norton: the same as a current source→Maximum power transfer (next)

Where this sits. Superposition showed that a linear circuit's response is a sum of simple parts. Thevenin's theorem uses that fact to shrink everything a load is connected to into two numbers, so changing the load never means re-solving the whole circuit.

Three terms first.

  • Terminals a–b: the two points where the load connects. Everything on the other side of them is the network.
  • Open-circuit voltage Voc: the voltage across a–b with the load removed (nothing connected).
  • Short-circuit current Isc: the current through a wire placed across a–b, counted from a to b through the wire (out of the + terminal).

Statement. Seen from a–b, any linear network behaves exactly like one voltage source Vth = Voc in series with one impedance Zth. Norton's form is the same network as one current source IN = Isc in parallel with ZN = Zth. The two forms are a source transformation of each other: Vth = INZth.

Finding Zth: three cases.

The network contains Zth is found by
Independent sources only switch every source off (V → short, I → open), then combine impedances seen from a–b
Independent and dependent sources Zth = Voc / Isc, or switch off the independent sources only and apply a test source
Dependent sources only Vth = 0; apply a test source (1 A in, measure V): Zth = V / I

With dependent sources Zth can come out negative (the network supplies energy). Keep the sign of Isc: it decides the sign of Zth.

A15 · Problem 5.15Thevenin · DC teach
Question

Draw the Thevenin's equivalent of the circuit in the figure and find the load current i. All values are in ohm.

Try it first

Remove R. Find the voltage across its terminals (two meshes), then short both sources and find the resistance seen from there. Last, put R back on the equivalent.

Hint: what's new
  • The Thevenin recipe: (1) remove the load; (2) Vth = open-circuit voltage at its terminals; (3) Rth = resistance seen into the terminals with every independent source switched off; (4) load current = Vth / (Rth + RL).
  • Switching off for Rth uses the same rule as superposition: voltage sources become shorts.

Given: 10 V, 5 V; 1 Ω (series with 10 V), 1 Ω, 1 Ω, 2 Ω; R = 2 Ω. To find: Vth, Rth, i.

Step 1: Vth (R removed). Mesh currents clockwise:

Mesh 1:3i1 − i2 = 10Mesh 2:−i1 + 4i2 = −5
⇒i1 = 3511 A,i2 = −511 A
Vth = Voc = 5 + 2i2 = 5 − 1011 = 4511 = 4.091 V

Step 2: Rth (both sources shorted):

(1 + 1) ∥ 1 = 23 Ω,23 + 1 = 53 Ω,Rth = 53 ∥ 2 = 1011 = 0.909 Ω

Step 3: load current:

i = VthRth + R = 45/1110/11 + 2 = 4532 A
Answer

Thevenin equivalent: 45/11 V in series with 10/11 Ω. i = 1.406 A (= book)

Side note

The book prints i1 = 5/11; it is 35/11 (only i2 is used, so the answer is unaffected). Full node solve with R in place: i = 1.40625 A ✓.

A16 · Problem 5.16Thevenin · dependent source teach
Question

Find I in the given figure, using Thevenin's theorem.

Try it first

The dependent source cannot be switched off, so Rth must come from Voc / Isc. Find both, and keep the sign of Isc.

Hint: what's new
  • Dependent source ⇒ Rth = Voc / Isc (or a test source). Shorting the independent sources and combining resistors would ignore the dependent source.
  • Isc is measured from x to y through the short. A negative Isc gives a negative Rth, which is allowed: the dependent source can supply energy.

Given: 10 V, 1 A, 1 Ω, VCVS 3V0, load 2 Ω. To find: I.

Voc (2 Ω removed). Nothing leaves at x, so the 1 A must flow left through the 1 Ω: V0 = 1 × 1 = 1 V.

Va = 10 + V0 = 11 V,Voc = Va − 3V0 = 11 − 3 = 8 V

Isc (x shorted to y, so Vx = 0):

0 = Va − 3V0 = (10 + V0) − 3V0⇒V0 = 5 V
KCL at a:1 = V01 + Isc⇒Isc = 1 − 5 = −4 A
Rth = VocIsc = 8−4 = −2 Ω

Load: Rth + 2 Ω = −2 + 2 = 0, so

I = VthRth + 2 = 80⇒no finite solution
Answer

Vth = 8 V, Rth = −2 Ω. With the 2 Ω load, Rth + RL = 0: the circuit as drawn has no solution. (Book: 2 A.)

Book error in 5.16

The book finds Isc = −4 A, then writes Rth = 8/4 = 2 Ω, dropping the minus sign, and prints I = 2 A. Direct check with the 2 Ω in place: KCL at a gives V0 = 1 − I; the right-hand path gives Vx = 10 − 2V0 = 8 + 2I; but Vx = 2I, so 8 = 0, a contradiction. A test source (10 V shorted, 1 A opened, 1 A pushed into x) confirms Rth = −2 Ω. For any other load, I = 8RL − 2.

A17 · Problem 5.17Thevenin · repeated reduction new idea
Question

By the iterative use of Thevenin's theorem, reduce the circuit shown in the figure to a single emf acting in series with a single resistor. Hence, calculate the current in the 10 Ω resistor connected across XY.

Try it first

Cut the ladder just right of the first shunt resistor and replace the left part by its Thevenin equivalent. Repeat, one rung at a time.

Hint: what's new
  • Iterative Thevenin: a ladder is reduced rung by rung. Each step is a voltage divider for Vth and a parallel combination for Rth: Vnew = Vold × RshRold + Rseries + Rsh, Rnew = (Rold + Rseries) ∥ Rsh.

Step 1 (left of AB: 100 V behind 90 + 10 = 100 Ω, shunt 1000 Ω):

V1 = 100 × 10001100 = 100011 V,R1 = 100 ∥ 1000 = 100011 Ω

Step 2 (add 100 Ω series, shunt 10 Ω):

V2 = 100011 × 102100/11 + 10 = 1000221 V,R2 = 210011 ∥ 10 = 2100221 Ω

Step 3 (add 100 Ω series, shunt 100 Ω):

V3 = 1000221 × 10024200/221 + 100 = 1000463 V,R3 = 24200221 ∥ 100 = 24200463 Ω

Step 4 (add 1000 Ω series):

Vth = 1000463 = 2.160 V,Rth = 24200463 + 1000 = 487200463 = 1052.3 Ω
I = 1000/463487200/463 + 10 = 1000491830 A
Answer

Single emf 2.160 V in series with 1052.3 Ω; I = 2.03 mA ≈ 0.002 A (= book)

A18 · Problem 5.18Thevenin · op-amp, test source new idea
Question

In the operational-amplifier circuit shown in the figure, find I in the R = 4 kΩ resistor, using Thevenin's theorem.

Try it first

With R removed, write KCL at e1 and at the inverting input. For Rth, short the 12 V and push 1 A into e1.

Hint: what's new
  • Ideal op-amp rules: no current into its inputs, and (with negative feedback) e2 = e+ = 0 V. The output can supply any current, so no KCL is written at the output node.
  • Test source for Rth: the op-amp acts like a dependent source, so switch off the 12 V only, inject 1 A at the terminals and read the voltage: Rth = e1 / 1 A.

Given: 12 V, 2 kΩ, 4 kΩ (feedback e1 → V0), 8 kΩ, 12 kΩ, ideal op-amp. To find: I in R = 4 kΩ.

Vth (R removed; e2 = 0, e3 = V0):

KCL at e2:0 − e18k + 0 − V012k = 0⇒V0 = −32e1
KCL at e1:e1 − 122k + e1 − V04k + e18k = 0⇒7e1 = 48 + 2V0
7e1 = 48 − 3e1⇒Vth = e1 = 4.8 V

Rth (12 V shorted, 1 A injected at e1):

e12k + e1 − V04k + e18k = 1⇒7e1 − 2V0 = 8000
10e1 = 8000⇒e1 = 800 V
Rth = 800 V1 A = 800 Ω,I = 4.8800 + 4000 = 1 × 10−3 A
Answer

Vth = 4.8 V, Rth = 800 Ω, I = 1 mA (= book)

A19 · Problem 5.19Thevenin · dependent current source practice
Question

Find Thevenin's equivalent about AB for the circuit shown in the figure.

Try it first

Voc: with AB open, what does KCL at the middle node say about Vs? Then short AB for Isc.

Voc (AB open, so the series 4 Ω carries nothing; Vs = 10 − VM). KCL at the middle node M:

Vs2 + 4Vs = 0⇒Vs = 0⇒Voc = VM = 10 V

Isc (AB shorted; V1 = VM, Vs = 10 − V1):

V1 − 102 + V14 = 4(10 − V1)⇒19V1 = 180⇒V1 = 9.474 V
Isc = V14 = 2.368 A
Rth = 102.368 = 4.22 Ω
Answer

Vth = 10 V, Rth = 38/9 = 4.22 Ω (= book)

Side note

The 2 Ω in series with the dependent current source never matters (5.1's shortcut). Test-source check (10 V shorted, 1 A into A): VA = 4 + 14.5 = 4.22 V ⇒ Rth = 4.22 Ω ✓.

A20 · Problem 5.20Thevenin · AC, floating terminals new idea
Question

In the network, determine the steady current in the 8 Ω inductor using Thevenin's theorem.

Try it first

With j8 removed, the circuit splits into two separate halves. Find Va and Vb with a divider each.

Hint: what's new
  • Neither terminal is ground. Vth = Va − Vb, each found from its own half.
  • With the sources shorted, each half is a parallel pair, and the two pairs are in series between a and b.
Va = 100∠0° × −j8j4 − j8 = 200∠0° V,Vb = 100∠60° × −j6j4 − j6 = 300∠60° V
Vth = Va − Vb = 200 − (150 + j259.81) = 50 − j259.81 = 264.58∠−79.11° V
Zth = (j4)(−j8)j4 − j8 + (j4)(−j6)j4 − j6 = j8 + j12 = j20 Ω
i = VthZth + j8 = 264.58∠−79.11°28∠90°

A21 · Problem 5.21Thevenin / Norton · AC, s-domain, dependent source new idea
Question

Obtain Thevenin's equivalent circuit with respect to terminals A–B in the networks shown below.

Try it first

(a)–(c) are practice. In (d), treat s like jω. In (e) the dependent source stays, so use Voc / Isc.

Hint: what's new
  • (d) s-domain: impedances are R, sL and 1sC; the source becomes its Laplace transform, 2 cos 2t → 2ss2 + 4. Everything else is unchanged.
  • (e) AC with a dependent source: find Vth and IN separately; Zth = Vth / IN.

(a)

Source transformation: 10∠0° A ∥ j15 Ω → j150 V in series with j15 Ω. With AB open, one loop:

I = j150j15 + 2 − j5 + 3 = j1505 + j10 = 13.42∠26.57° A,Vth = I × (−j5) = 30 − j60 V
Zth = (−j5) ∥ (5 + j15) = −j5(5 + j15)5 + j10 = 1 − j7 Ω
Answer

(a) Vth = 67.08∠−63.43° V, Zth = 7.07∠−81.87° Ω (= book)

(b)

Vth = 20∠90° × 3 − j4(5 + j10) + (3 − j4) = j20(3 − j4)8 + j6 = 100∠36.87°10∠36.87° = 10∠0° V
Zth = (5 + j10)(3 − j4)8 + j6 = 55 + j108 + j6 = 5 − j2.5 Ω
Answer

(b) Vth = 10∠0° V, Zth = 5.59∠−26.57° Ω (= book; its first line prints j120, a typo for j20)

(c) The 4 Ω across AB is the load.

Z = 10 + (−j5) ∥ (13 + j6) = 11.91 − j5.15 = 12.98∠−23.37° Ω
I = 100Z = 7.706∠23.37° A
Iright = I × −j513 + j1 = 2.955∠−71.03° A,Vth = Iright(8 + j6) = 29.55∠−34.16° V
Zth = [(10 ∥ −j5) + 5] ∥ (8 + j6) = (7 − j4) ∥ (8 + j6) = 5.328 − j0.044 Ω
Answer

(c) Vth = 29.55∠−34.16° V, Zth = 5.33∠−0.47° Ω (= book)

(d)

The two 14 F capacitors both run from the same node to ground, so they add: 12 F → 2s. A is the node after the inductor; B is ground.

Vth(s) = 2ss2 + 4 × 1 + 2/s(1 + 2/s) + (1 + s/2) = 2ss2 + 4 × 2s + 2 = 4s(s2 + 4)(s + 2)

(Simplify: 1 + 2/s = s + 2s and 2 + s/2 + 2/s = (s + 2)22s, so the ratio is 2s + 2.)

Zth(s) = (1 + 2/s) ∥ (1 + s/2) = (s + 2)2/(2s)(s + 2)2/(2s) = 1 Ω
Answer

(d) Vth(s) = 4s(s2 + 4)(s + 2) V, Zth = 1 Ω (= book)

(e)

Vth. With AB open, the 5I circulates only through the −j5 Ω, so the source current is set by the left loop alone:

I = 10∠0°100 + j10 = 0.0995∠−5.71° A
Vth = VAB = I(j10) − 5I(−j5) = j35I = 3.483∠84.29° V

IN. AB shorted. Right loop: j10(I − IN) + j25I + j5IN = 0 ⇒ IN = 7I. Left loop:

10 = (100 + j10)I − j10IN = (100 − j60)I⇒I = 0.0857∠30.96° A
IN = 7I = 0.600∠30.96° A
Zth = VthIN = 3.483∠84.29°0.600∠30.96° = 5.80∠53.33° Ω
Answer

(e) Vth = 3.48∠84.3° V, IN = 0.600∠31.0° A, Zth = 5.80∠53.3° Ω (= book)

A22 · Problem 5.22Thevenin · AC, dependent source practice
Question

Find V0 using Thevenin's theorem.

Try it first

ω = 1: work out the three reactances first. Transform 3i0 ∥ j2 into a voltage source, then write two mesh equations for each of Vth and IN.

Reactances (ω = 1): 2 H → j2 Ω, 14 F → −j4 Ω, 18 F → −j8 Ω.

Vth (2 Ω removed; clockwise mesh currents, i0 = I1):

Mesh 1:(4 − j4)I1 + j4I2 = −12
Mesh 2:−j4(I2 − I1) + j2I2 − j6I1 − j8I2 = 0⇒−j2I1 − j10I2 = 0⇒I2 = −0.2I1
(4 − j4.8)I1 = −12⇒I1 = −1.230 − j1.475 A,I2 = 0.246 + j0.295 A
Vth = I2(−j8) = 2.361 − j1.967 = 3.073∠−39.81° V

IN (terminals shorted):

Mesh 2:−j4(I2 − I1) + j2I2 − j6I1 = 0⇒I2 = −I1;(4 − j8)I1 = −12
IN = I2 = 124 − j8 = 0.6 + j1.2 = 1.342∠63.43° A
Zth = VthIN = 2.290∠−103.24° = −0.525 − j2.230 Ω
V0 = Vth × 2Zth + 2 = 3.073∠−39.81° × 22.674∠−56.50° = 2.299∠16.70° V
Answer

V0 = 2.30∠16.70° V, i.e. v0(t) = 2.30 cos(t + 16.70°) V

Book error in 5.22

For Vth, the book writes mesh 2 as −j2I1 − j6I2 = 0: it keeps the shared −j4 in the I1 term but drops it from I2's own impedance (−j4 + j2 − j8 = −j10, not −j6). That gives Vth = 4.8∠−36.87° V, Zth = 3.58∠−100.3° Ω and V0 = 1.27∠32° V. Its IN = 1.342∠63.43° A is right. The answer above was confirmed by a full node solve with the 2 Ω in place (2.2988∠16.70° V).

A23 · Problem 5.23Norton · DC new idea
Question

Obtain the Norton's equivalent circuit with respect to the terminals AB for the network shown in the figure.

Try it first

Short A to B. What current does each source push through the short?

Hint: what's new
  • Norton's form: IN = Isc (current through the A–B short), RN = Rth, drawn as a current source in parallel with RN, arrow pointing towards A.
  • With A–B shorted, each source sees only its own resistor, so Isc is a sum of two Ohm's-law currents.
RN = 5 ∥ 15 = 7520 = 3.75 Ω
IN = Isc = 105 + 2015 = 2 + 1.333 = 3.33 A

A24 · Problem 5.24Norton · from a v–i characteristic new idea
Question

For the one-port shown in the figure, determine the Norton's equivalent at the terminals AB, if the v–i characteristic is given by 16v = 80 − 2i.

Try it first

Which two points on the v–i line are Voc and Isc?

Hint: what's new
  • The equivalent is read off the terminal line. i = 0 gives Voc; v = 0 gives Isc; RN = Voc / Isc (the size of the line's slope, Δv/Δi).
16v = 80 − 2i⇒v5 + i40 = 1
i = 0:Voc = 5 Vv = 0:Isc = 40 ARN = 540 = 18 Ω
Answer

IN = 40 A (towards A) in parallel with RN = 1/8 Ω (= book)

Sign convention

v = 5 − i8 describes an ordinary source only if i is the current delivered out of A (v falls as the load draws more). The figure's arrow points into N; read literally, that would make RN = −1/8 Ω with the 40 A reversed. The intended answer is the book's.

A25 · Problem 5.25Thevenin + Norton · superposition inside practice
Question

Find both Thevenin's and Norton's equivalent circuits for the network shown in the figure. All values are in ohm.

Try it first

Which resistors does the shorted 5 V source remove from Rth? Then find Isc one source at a time.

RN = Rth = (2 ∥ 1) + 1 = 23 + 1 = 53 Ω

Vm − 52 + Vm1 + Vm1 = 0⇒Vm = 1 V,Isc′ = 11 = 1 A

Isc, 2 A alone (5 V shorted): the 2 A divides between 2 Ω ∥ 1 Ω = 2/3 Ω and the 1 Ω to the short:

IN = 1 + 45 = 95 A,Vth = INRth = 95 × 53 = 3 V

A26 · Problem 5.26Thevenin · dependent source practice
Question

Replace the circuit in the figure with the Thevenin's equivalent circuit across A and B.

Book error in 5.26: figure and solution belong to different circuits

The figure shows no A and B, so the question cannot be answered as printed. The book's solution solves a different circuit (a transistor model): 10 mV source, 1 kΩ carrying I, a controlled voltage 10−4V0 in the input loop, and a controlled current source 75I in parallel with 30 kΩ across A–B. That solution is checked below. Ask your professor which circuit is meant before submitting.

Voc (A–B open). The 75I pulls current down out of node A, and it can only return through the 30 kΩ, so V0 = 30k × (−75I) = −2.25 × 106I. Input loop:

103I + 10−4V0 = 10 × 10−3⇒−4.444 × 10−4V0 + 1 × 10−4V0 = 10−2⇒V0 = −29.03 V

Isc. A–B shorted ⇒ V0 = 0, so I = 10 mV1 kΩ = 10−5 A and Isc = −75I = −7.5 × 10−4 A.

Rth = −29.03−7.5 × 10−4 = 38.71 kΩ

A27 · Problem 5.27Thevenin · dependent sources, negative Rth practice
Question

Find the Thevenin's equivalent between terminals a and b of the circuit shown in the figure.

Try it first

Vx = Voc feeds back into the left loop. For Isc, Vx = 0 removes the 2Vx source.

Voc (R = 50 kΩ, as in the question figure). Left loop and right node:

I0 = 3 − 2Vx1000,Voc = Vx = −40I0 × 50000 = −2000(3 − 2Voc)
3999Voc = 6000⇒Voc = 1.5004 V

Isc (Vx = 0 ⇒ 2Vx = 0): I0 = 31000 = 3 mA. The 50 kΩ is shorted, and the dependent source pulls 40I0 from a down to b, so the short carries it from b to a:

Isc (a → b) = −40I0 = −0.12 A,Rth = 1.5004−0.12 = −12.50 Ω
Answer

Vth = 1.500 V, Rth = −12.50 Ω (figure value 50 kΩ)

Book errors in 5.27
  1. The solution uses 50 Ω (Vx = −40I0 × 50 = −2000I0), not the figure's 50 kΩ. With 50 Ω: Voc = −2(3 − 2Voc) ⇒ Voc = 2 V.
  2. It then writes Rth = 2/0.12 = 16.67 Ω, dropping the sign of Isc = −0.12 A. With 50 Ω the correct value is Rth = −16.67 Ω.

Test-source check (3 V shorted, 1 V applied at a): I0 = −21000 A, current drawn = 1R − 0.08, giving Rth = −12.50 Ω (50 kΩ) or −16.67 Ω (50 Ω) ✓.

A28 · Problem 5.28Norton · s-domain transient new idea
Question

In the network shown in the figure, the switch is closed at time t = 0. Assuming all the initial currents and voltages as zero, find the current through the inductor L2 by the use of Norton's theorem.

Try it first

Draw the s-domain circuit (zero initial conditions). Make (R2 + sL2) the load and find the Norton equivalent of the rest.

Hint: what's new
  • Transient = theorem in the s-domain. A DC source switched on at t = 0 becomes Vs; R → R, L → sL, C → 1sC. Find IL(s) exactly as in AC, then invert with partial fractions.
  • With A–B shorted the capacitor is shorted out, so Isc is one Ohm's-law step.

s-domain: source 3s; R1 + sL1 = s + 2; C = 2 F → 12s; load R2 + sL2 = s + 2.

ZN = (s + 2) ∥ 12s = s + 22s2 + 4s + 1,IN = Isc = 3/ss + 2 = 3s(s + 2)
IL(s) = IN × ZNZN + (s + 2) = 3s(s + 2) × 11 + (2s2 + 4s + 1) = 32s(s + 2)(s + 1)2
Partial fractions:IL(s) = 3/4s − 3/4s + 2 + 0s + 1 − 3/2(s + 1)2

(Coefficients: at s = 0, 32·2·1 = 34; at s = −2, 32(−2)(1) = −34; on (s + 1)2, 32(−1)(1) = −32; on 1/(s + 1), 0, because the s3 terms must cancel.)

Answer

iL2(t) = 34 − 34e−2t − 32te−t A (t ≥ 0)

Book error in 5.28

The figure gives C = 2 F, but the book's s-domain network uses 1s (that is C = 1 F) and prints i(t) = 34 − 34e−2t − 32e−t sin t A. That answer is right for a 1 F capacitor only. A direct simulation of the circuit equations with C = 2 F matches the answer above (e.g. i(1 s) = 0.0967 A; the book's formula gives 0.184 A). Checks: i(0) = 0 and i(∞) = 32 + 2 = 0.75 A.

In the network of the figure, the switch K is closed at time t = 0, a steady state having previously existed. Obtain the current in the resistor R using Thevenin's theorem.

A31 · Problem 5.31Thevenin · symbolic, two dependent sources new idea
Question

For the network shown in the figure, show that the Thevenin equivalent at the terminals a-b is represented by VTh = V12(1 + a + b − ab) and ZTh = 3 − b2.

Try it first

Keep a, b and V1 as letters. Open circuit: no current in the right 1 Ω. Short circuit: two mesh equations.

A34 · Problem 5.34Thevenin · no independent source new idea
Question

Find Thevenin's equivalent circuit for the network shown in the figure.

Try it first

There is nothing to drive the circuit. What is Vth? For Zth, connect a 1 A source and find the voltage it produces.

Hint: what's new
  • Only dependent sources: Vth = 0 (no independent source, no response), and Isc = 0 too, so Voc/Isc fails. Use a test source: Zth = V / I.
KCL at x:V − v010 − 0.5v0 − I = 0⇒V = 10I + 6v0
Current down the 20 Ω = V − v010 = 0.5v0 + I
v0 = 20(0.5v0 + I)⇒v0 = −209I
V = 10I − 1209I = −103I⇒Zth = −3.33 Ω
Answer

Vth = 0, Zth = −10/3 = −3.33 Ω (= book; its final sketch omits the minus sign)

C · Maximum power transfer theorem

Thevenin / Norton (done)→Load sees only Vth and Zth→Maximum power: choose the load to match Zth

Where this sits. Thevenin's theorem reduced any network to Vth in series with Zth. The load current is then Vth / (Zth + ZL), so the only question left is which load draws the most power from that one source.

Three terms first.

  • Load: the element connected at the terminals, RL (DC) or ZL = RL + jXL (AC).
  • Average power in the load: P = |I|2RL. Only the resistive part of the load absorbs power.
  • Complex conjugate: for Zth = Rth + jXth, the conjugate is Zth* = Rth − jXth (same resistance, opposite reactance).

Statement.

Load allowed to vary Maximum power when Pmax
RL only, DC RL = Rth Vth24Rth
ZL = RL + jXL, both free (AC) ZL = Zth* (reactances cancel) |Vth|24Rth
Pure resistance RL, AC source RL = |Zth| |I|2RL (calculate)

The recipe is always: find Vth and Zth, then match. At maximum power the load gets exactly half the power, so efficiency is only 50%.

Phasor size convention. The book takes phasor magnitudes as rms values, so P = |Vth|2 / (4Rth). If a source is given as a peak value, the power is half of that.

A35 · Problem 5.35Power and superposition new idea
Question

In the network shown, the power dissipated in R when E1, E2 or E3 acting alone is (a) 20 W, 80 W and 5 W respectively; (b) 30 W, 270 W and 120 W respectively. Calculate the maximum power that R can dissipate due to the simultaneous action of all the sources. Calculate both for (a) and (b). What will be the minimum power dissipated in R when all the sources are acting simultaneously?

Try it first

Power does not add. What does add? Turn each power back into a current, and remember you don't know each current's sign.

Hint: what's new
  • Superposition adds currents, not powers. Each source alone gives |ik| = √(Pk/R); the directions are unknown, so the total is ±i1 ± i2 ± i3.
  • P = i2R = (±√(P1) ± √(P2) ± √(P3))2. Largest: all signs the same. Smallest: the sign choice that makes the sum closest to zero.
i = ±√(P1R) ± √(P2R) ± √(P3R)⇒P = i2R = (±√(P1) ± √(P2) ± √(P3))2

(a) √(20) = 2√(5), √(80) = 4√(5), √(5):

Pmax = (2 + 4 + 1)2 × 5 = 49 × 5 = 245 W,Pmin = (4 − 2 − 1)2 × 5 = 5 W

(b) √(30), √(270) = 3√(30), √(120) = 2√(30):

Pmax = (1 + 3 + 2)2 × 30 = 36 × 30 = 1080 W,Pmin = (3 − 1 − 2)2 × 30 = 0 W
Answer

(a) Pmax = 245 W, Pmin = 5 W. (b) Pmax = 1080 W, Pmin = 0 W (= book)

Side note

Adding the powers would give 105 W and 420 W, which is wrong in both cases. The book's working line for (b) Pmax misprints the bracket as [4√(5) − 3√(5)]; its answer 1080 W is right.

A36 · Problem 5.36Maximum power · DC teach
Question

Find the value of R in the circuit of the figure such that maximum power transfer takes place. What is the amount of this power?

Try it first

For each circuit: remove R, find Vth across its terminals and Rth looking back in. Then R = Rth and Pmax = Vth2/(4Rth). In (b), look for an element that changes nothing. In (c), R is not connected to ground.

Hint: what's new
  • Maximum power transfer (DC): R = Rth, Pmax = Vth24Rth. All the work is in finding Vth and Rth.
  • (b) the 2 Ω directly across the 5 V source changes no other current (5.1's shortcut); then source transformations reduce the rest.
  • (c) R sits between two non-ground nodes, so Vth = VP − VQ.

(a)

Vth. Mesh currents with R removed: 3i1 − 2i2 = 4, −2i1 + 8i2 = 0 ⇒ i1 = 4i2, so 10i2 = 4:

i2 = 25 A,Vth = 1 × i2 + 6 = 325 = 6.4 V
Rth = [(1 ∥ 2) + 5] ∥ 1 = 173 ∥ 1 = 1720 = 0.85 Ω
Pmax = Vth24Rth = 6.424 × 0.85 = 40.963.4 = 12.05 W
Answer

(a) R = 0.85 Ω, Pmax = 12.05 W (= book, which rounds to 12 W)

(b)

Combine the two current sources and the two resistors, then transform back:

53 + 2 = 113 A,3 ∥ 1 = 34 Ω⇒113 × 34 = 114 V in series with 34 Ω
Vth = 114 V,Rth = 34 + 1 = 74 Ω,Pmax = (11/4)24 × 7/4 = 121112 = 1.08 W
Answer

(b) R = 7/4 = 1.75 Ω, Pmax = 1.08 W (= book)

(c)

Rth = 2 + (10 ∥ 5) = 2 + 103 = 5.33 Ω

Vth. With R removed, no current flows in the 2 Ω, so VP = 10 V. The right loop gives VQ = 24 × 515 = 8 V (the book writes this as i = −24/15 = −1.6 A, Voc = 5i + 10).

Vth = VP − VQ = 10 − 8 = 2 V,Pmax = 224 × 16/3 = 316 = 0.1875 W
Answer

(c) R = 5.33 Ω, Pmax = 0.1875 W (= book, 0.188 W)

Check

For each part, the full circuit was solved with R swept from 0 to 50 Ω; the power peaks at the R and Pmax above.

A37 · Problem 5.37Maximum power · AC conjugate match new idea
Question

In the network shown, find the value of ZL to which the maximum power can be delivered. Hence, find the value of the maximum power.

Try it first

Find Vth and Zth at A–B as in any AC Thevenin problem. Then choose ZL so that the total impedance in the loop is purely resistive.

Hint: what's new
  • AC load free in R and X: ZL = Zth*. The reactances cancel (XL = −Xth), leaving the DC case RL = Rth, so Pmax = |Vth|24Rth.

Vth. Impedance seen by the source: 3 + j3 ∥ (3 − j3) = 3 + (3 + j3) = 6 + j3 Ω.

I = 56 + j3,Iright = I × j3j3 + 3 − j3 = jI
Vth = Iright(−j3) = 3I = 156 + j3 = 2 − j1 = 2.236∠−26.57° V

Zth (source shorted):

3 ∥ j3 = 1.5 + j1.5,(1.5 + j1.5 + 3) ∥ (−j3) = (4.5 + j1.5)(−j3)4.5 − j1.5 = 1.8 − j2.4 Ω
ZL = Zth* = 1.8 + j2.4 Ω,I = Vth2 × 1.8 = 0.621∠−26.57° A
Pmax = 2.23624 × 1.8 = 0.694 W
Answer

ZL = 1.8 + j2.4 Ω, Pmax = 0.694 W (= book)

A38 · Problem 5.38Maximum power · AC load impedance practice
Question

A loudspeaker is connected across terminals A and B of the network. What should be its impedance to obtain maximum power dissipation in it?

Try it first

Only Zth is needed: switch the sources off and look back from A–B.

(a)

Zth = (3 + j4)(−j5)3 + j4 − j5 = 20 − j153 − j1 = 7.5 − j2.5 = 7.91∠−18.43° Ω
Answer

(a) ZL = Zth* = 7.5 + j2.5 Ω (the book prints 7.5 + j2.4, a typo; its own Zth is 7.5 − j2.5)

(b)

(10 + j8) ∥ j5 = −40 + j5010 + j13 = 0.929 + j3.792 Ω
+ (4 + j6) = 4.929 + j9.792 Ω,∥ 10 Ω⇒Zth = 5.316 + j3.072 = 6.14∠30° Ω
Answer

(b) ZL = Zth* = 5.316 − j3.072 = 6.14∠−30° Ω (= book)

A39 · Problem 5.39Maximum power · resistive load on an AC source new idea
Question

Two inductors each of 1 Ω reactance and negligible resistance are connected in series across a 2 V a.c. source. Find the value of resistance which should be connected across one of the inductors for maximum power dissipation. Also, find the maximum power.

Try it first

Draw it: 2 V source, j1, then j1 ∥ R. Write the power in R as a function of R and maximise it, or find the Thevenin equivalent seen by R first.

Hint: what's new
  • Only a resistance is allowed, so the reactance cannot be cancelled and ZL = Zth* is impossible. For a purely resistive load the best value is R = |Zth|.

Route 1: calculus (as the book):

Z = jRR + j1 + j1 = −1 + j2RR + j1,IR = 2(R + j1)−1 + j2R × j1R + j1 = j2−1 + j2R
P = |IR|2R = 4R1 + 4R2,dPdR = 4(1 + 4R2) − 4R(8R)(1 + 4R2)2 = 0⇒4 − 16R2 = 0⇒R = 0.5 Ω
Pmax = 4 × 0.51 + 4 × 0.25 = 1 W

Route 2: Thevenin. Seen by R: Vth = 2 × j1j1 + j1 = 1 V, Zth = j1 ∥ j1 = j0.5 Ω. Pure resistance ⇒ R = |Zth| = 0.5 Ω, and |I|2 = 1|0.5 + j0.5|2 = 2, so P = 2 × 0.5 = 1 W ✓.

Answer

R = 0.5 Ω, Pmax = 1 W (= book; its last line prints 4 × 0.4, a typo for 4 × 0.5)

A40 · Problem 5.40Maximum power · dependent source practice
Question

In the network shown, calculate the maximum power that may be dissipated in the external resistor R.

Try it first

The dependent source rules out "switch off and combine", so find Voc and Isc. Start by turning 10 A ∥ 4 Ω into a voltage source.

Voc (no current in the 3 Ω, so the loop current is i1):

−40 + 4i1 − 2i1 + 6i1 = 0⇒i1 = 5 A,Voc = 6i1 = 30 V

Isc. Let VM be the node above the 6 Ω: i1 = VM/6, Isc = VM/3, source current = VM/6 + VM/3 = VM/2. Left loop:

40 − 4 × VM2 + 2 × VM6 − VM = 0⇒83VM = 40
VM = 15 V,Isc = 153 = 5 A
Rth = 305 = 6 Ω,Pmax = 3024 × 6 = 37.5 W
Answer

R = 6 Ω, Pmax = 37.5 W (= book)

A41 · Problem 5.41Maximum power · AC practice
Question

Find the Thevenin's equivalent between the points a and b for the circuit given in the figure. What should be the value of impedance connected between a and b for maximum power to be transferred from the sources? Obtain the amount of the maximum power.

I = 1002 + 3 + j5 = 10 − j10 A,Vth = I(3 + j5) = 80 + j20 = 82.46∠14.04° V
Zth = j6 + 2(3 + j5)5 + j5 = j6 + 1.6 + j0.4 = 1.6 + j6.4 Ω
ZL = Zth* = 1.6 − j6.4 Ω,Pmax = |Vth|24Rth = 68004 × 1.6 = 1062.5 W
Answer

Vth = 82.46∠14.04° V, Zth = 1.6 + j6.4 Ω; ZL = 1.6 − j6.4 Ω, Pmax = 1062.5 W (= book)

A42 · Problem 5.42Maximum power · AC, two sources practice
Question

In the network in the figure, two voltage sources act on the load impedance connected to the terminal A and B. If the load is variable in both reactance and resistance, for what load ZL will receive maximum power? What is the value of maximum power?

Vth (ZL removed; one loop current from the 50 V towards the j25 V):

I = 50 − j25(5 + j5) + (3 − j4) = 50 − j258 + j1
Vth = 50 − I(5 + j5) = 25 − j758 + j1 = 1.923 − j9.615 = 9.806∠−78.69° V
Zth = (5 + j5)(3 − j4)8 + j1 = 35 − j58 + j1 = 4.231 − j1.154 Ω
ZL = Zth* = 4.231 + j1.154 Ω,Pmax = 9.80624 × 4.231 = 96.1516.92 = 5.68 W
Answer

ZL = 4.23 + j1.154 Ω, Pmax = 5.68 W (= book to rounding: it squares 9.8 and prints 5.676 W)

A43 · Problem 5.43Maximum power · equivalent from measurements new idea
Question

A network has two output terminals. The open circuit voltage at these terminals is 260 V. The current flowing through the terminals is 20 A when the terminals are short circuited. Also, the current is 13 A when a coil of 11 ohm reactance and negligible resistance is connected across the terminals. Find the impedance components of the equivalent circuit feeding the terminals. What value of load impedance will give maximum power transfer and what is the value of this power?

Try it first

Let Zth = R + jX. The two current readings give two equations for the magnitudes |R + jX| and |R + j(X + 11)|.

Hint: what's new
  • Zth from terminal measurements: |Zth| = Voc/Isc gives R2 + X2; a known reactance added in series gives a second equation. Subtracting them isolates X.
|Zth| = 26020 = 13 Ω⇒R2 + X2 = 169…(i)
260|R + j(X + 11)| = 13⇒R2 + (X + 11)2 = 400…(ii)
(ii) − (i):22X + 121 = 231⇒X = 5 Ω,R = √(169 − 25) = 12 Ω
ZL = Zth* = 12 − j5 Ω,Pmax = 26024 × 12 = 1408.3 W
Answer

Zth = 12 + j5 Ω; ZL = 12 − j5 Ω, Pmax = 1408.3 W (= book)

Check

260/|12 + j5| = 260/13 = 20 A ✓; 260/|12 + j16| = 260/20 = 13 A ✓.

A44 · Problem 5.44Maximum power · AC, two sources practice
Question

What should be the value of ZL for maximum power to be delivered in the circuit shown in the figure?

Zth = (3 + j2) ∥ (4 − j3) = (3 + j2)(4 − j3)7 − j1 = 18 − j17 − j1 = 127 + j1150 = 2.54 + j0.22 Ω
Answer

ZL = Zth* = 2.54 − j0.22 = 2.55∠−4.95° Ω (= book)

Side note

The source values do not affect ZL; they only set Vth and hence Pmax. Thevenin's equivalent works here because both sources share one frequency ω.

Part B · Sadiku (unsolved problems)

Alexander & Sadiku, Fundamentals of Electric Circuits 5e, ch. 4 "Circuit Theorems": practice problems, then end-of-chapter problems
Part A: every method, solved (done)→Part B: same theorems, your turn→Superposition §4.3→Source transformation §4.4→Thevenin / Norton §4.5–4.6→Max power §4.8

Where this sits. Part A taught every method on solved problems. Sadiku's problems are unsolved, so they are practice: the solutions here are compact, and an orange hint appears only when a problem adds something Part A did not show.

Answers. Practice problems print their answer beside the question ("= book"). End-of-chapter problems have answers only for odd numbers, in Appendix D ("= App. D"). Every answer here, odd or even, was checked by solving the full circuit with all sources on, and every superposition part was checked to add up to it.

A · Superposition (§4.3)

B1 · Practice Problem 4.3Superposition · DC practice
Question

Using the superposition theorem, find vo in the circuit of Fig. 4.8.

5 A alone (12 V shorted). From the middle node the 5 A sees 3 + 2 = 5 Ω and 5 Ω, so it splits 2.5 A each way:

vo′ = 2.5 × 2 = 5 V

12 V alone (5 A opened). 5 Ω, 3 Ω and 2 Ω in series:

i = 125 + 3 + 2 = 1.2 A⇒vo″ = 1.2 × 2 = 2.4 V
Answer

vo = 5 + 2.4 = 7.4 V (= book)

B2 · Practice Problem 4.4Superposition · dependent current source practice
Question

Use superposition to find vx in the circuit of Fig. 4.11.

Try it first

The dependent source stays in both cases. One KCL at the vx node per case.

25 V alone (5 A opened):

25 − vx′20 + 0.1vx′ = vx′4⇒1.25 = 0.2vx′⇒vx′ = 6.25 V

5 A alone (25 V shorted):

5 + 0.1vx″ = vx″4 + vx″20⇒5 = 0.2vx″⇒vx″ = 25 V

B3 · Practice Problem 4.5Superposition · three sources practice
Question

Find I in the circuit of Fig. 4.14 using the superposition principle.

With the other sources off, the loop is always 6 + 2 + 8 = 16 Ω.

8 V alone:I′ = 816 = 0.5 A6 V alone (it opposes I):I″ = −616 = −0.375 A
2 A alone (2 A ∥ 2 Ω → 4 V in series with 2 Ω, pushing to the right):I‴ = 416 = 0.25 A

B4 · Problem 4.8Superposition · one-node circuit new idea
Question

Using superposition, find Vo in the circuit of Fig. 4.76. Check with PSpice or MultiSim.

Hint: what's new
  • One-node shortcut. When every branch meets at one node, write one KCL at that node in each case instead of chaining dividers. Here the branches from Vo are 4 + 5 = 9 Ω, 3 Ω (+ 9 V) and 1 Ω (+ 3 V).

9 V alone (3 V shorted):

Vo′9 + Vo′ − 93 + Vo′1 = 0⇒139Vo′ = 3⇒Vo′ = 2713 V

3 V alone (9 V shorted):

Vo″9 + Vo″3 + Vo″ − 31 = 0⇒139Vo″ = 3⇒Vo″ = 2713 V
Answer

Vo = 5413 = 4.154 V (even problem; full node solve agrees. The book's PSpice/MultiSim check is replaced by that solve.)

B5 · Problem 4.9Superposition + linearity new idea
Question

Given that I = 4 amps when Vs = 40 volts and Is = 4 amps and I = 1 amp when Vs = 20 volts and Is = 0, use superposition and linearity to determine the value of I when Vs = 60 volts and Is = −2 amps.

Hint: what's new
  • Superposition without the circuit values. In a linear circuit any response is a weighted sum of the sources, I = aVs + bIs. The two measurements give two equations for a and b.
Is = 0:1 = 20a⇒a = 0.05
4 = 40(0.05) + 4b⇒b = 0.5
I = 0.05 × 60 + 0.5 × (−2) = 3 − 1 = 2 A
Answer

I = 2 A (= App. D)

B6 · Problem 4.10Superposition · design problem new idea
Question

Using Fig. 4.78, design a problem to help other students better understand superposition. Note, the letter k is a gain you can specify to make the problem easier to solve but must not be zero.

Hint: what's new
  • Design problem: there is no single answer. Choose values, then solve your own problem. Below is one complete design; any other non-zero choice is equally valid.

One design. In Fig. 4.78 (V in series with R and the dependent source kVab, current source I across a–b), take V = 12 V, R = 4 Ω, I = 3 A, k = 2, and ask: use superposition to find Vab.

Solution. Terminals a–b are open, so the current I must return through R and the source V: the series current from V towards a is −I. KVL around the loop: V − R(−I) − kVab = Vab, so in general Vab = V + RI1 + k.

12 V alone (I = 0):Vab′ = 121 + 2 = 4 V3 A alone (V = 0):Vab″ = 4 × 31 + 2 = 4 V
Answer

(this design) Vab = 4 + 4 = 8 V (design problem; the book lists "multiple answers")

B7 · Problem 4.11Superposition · dependent source practice
Question

Use the superposition principle to find io and vo in the circuit of Fig. 4.79.

Let the middle node be M and the left node A. KCL at M in either case: 5io flows on through the 20 Ω.

6 A alone (30 V shorted): 5io = VM/20 ⇒ VM = 100io, VA = VM + 10io = 110io.

KCL at A:6 = 110io40 + io = 3.75io⇒io′ = 1.6 A,vo′ = 16 V

30 V alone (6 A opened; the right end of the 20 Ω is at −30 V): VM = 100io − 30, VA = 110io − 30.

0 = 110io − 3040 + io⇒3.75io = 0.75⇒io″ = 0.2 A,vo″ = 2 V

B8 · Problem 4.12Superposition · three sources practice
Question

Determine vo in the circuit of Fig. 4.80 using the superposition principle.

12 V alone. B sees 12 ∥ 4 = 3 Ω; A sees 3 ∥ (5 + 3) = 2411 Ω.

VA = 12 × 24/116 + 24/11 = 3.2 V,VB = 3.2 × 38 = 1.2 V,vo′ = 2 V

B9 · Problem 4.13Superposition · three sources practice
Question

Use superposition to find vo in the circuit of Fig. 4.81.

2 A alone. It splits between 10 Ω and 8 + 5 = 13 Ω:

i5Ω = 2 × 1023 = 2023 A,vo′ = 5 × 2023 = 10023 V

i = −1223 A,vo″ = 5i = −6023 V

B10 · Problem 4.14Superposition · three sources practice
Question

Apply the superposition principle to find vo in the circuit of Fig. 4.82.

20 V alone. Between the rails: 6 Ω ∥ (4 + 2) Ω = 3 Ω, then 3 Ω to ground: vo′ = 20 × 36 = 10 V.

1 A alone. From the middle node: 4 Ω to ground, or 2 Ω + (3 ∥ 6 = 2 Ω). Current towards the right rail = 1 × 44 + 4 = 0.5 A: vo‴ = 0.5 × 2 = 1 V.

B11 · Problem 4.15Superposition · power practice
Question

For the circuit in Fig. 4.83, use superposition to find i. Calculate the power delivered to the 3-Ω resistor.

20 V alone. The top node sees 4 Ω (1 + 3) and 4 Ω (right): 2 Ω. VT = 20 × 22 + 2 = 10 V, i′ = 104 = 2.5 A.

2 A alone. The 2 A enters the 3 Ω node and returns to the top node either through 1 Ω or through 3 Ω + (2 ∥ 4 = 43 Ω): i″ = 2 × 11 + 13/3 = 0.375 A.

16 V alone. The bottom of the right 4 Ω sits at −16 V; the top node sees 2 ∥ 4 = 43 Ω: VT = −16 × 4/34/3 + 4 = −4 V, i‴ = −1 A.

i = 2.5 + 0.375 − 1 = 1.875 A,P3Ω = i2 × 3 = 10.55 W

Power does not superpose

Adding the three partial powers (18.75 + 0.42 + 3 W) gives a wrong answer. Add the currents first, then square.

B12 · Problem 4.16Superposition · three sources practice
Question

Given the circuit in Fig. 4.84, use superposition to obtain i0.

12 V alone. Seen from the 4 Ω: 10 ∥ (3 + 2 + 5) = 5 Ω, so i0′ = 124 + 5 = 43 A.

2 A alone. From its node: 5 Ω to ground, or 2 + 3 + (4 ∥ 10 = 207) Ω. Current towards the 10 Ω node = 2 × 55 + 5 + 20/7 = 79 A, so VA = 79 × 207 = 209 V and i0″ = −VA4 = −59 A.

Use superposition to obtain vx in the circuit of Fig. 4.85. Check your result using PSpice or MultiSim.

B14 · Problem 4.18Superposition · dependent current source practice
Question

Use superposition to find Vo in the circuit of Fig. 4.86.

B15 · Problem 4.19Superposition · floating dependent source new idea
Question

Use superposition to solve for vx in the circuit of Fig. 4.87.

Hint: what's new
  • A dependent source in the return wire. The bottom wire is split into two nodes that differ by 4ix. Take the left bottom node as ground; then the right bottom node is at 4ix, and vx = Vtop − 4ix.

With ix = Vtop/2: vx = Vtop − 2Vtop = −Vtop. KCL at the top node (sources entering = currents leaving):

Iin = Vtop2 + vx8 = Vtop2 − Vtop8 = 38Vtop
6 A alone:6 = 38Vtop⇒Vtop = 16 V,vx′ = −16 V
4 A alone:4 = 38Vtop⇒Vtop = 10.67 V,vx″ = −10.67 V

vx = −16 − 10.67 = −26.67 V (= App. D)

B · Source transformation (§4.4)

Superposition (done)→Source transformation: swap V + series R ↔ I ∥ R→Thevenin / Norton (next)

Where this sits. Part A used source transformation inside superposition cases (5.9, 5.10). Here it is the whole method: keep swapping sources until the circuit is one loop or one node.

The rule. A voltage source Vs in series with R is equivalent to a current source is = Vs/R in parallel with the same R, and back again. The current source's arrow points towards the voltage source's + terminal.

  • It works for dependent sources too, as long as the controlling voltage or current is not hidden inside the swap.
  • A source with no series R (voltage) or no parallel R (current) cannot be transformed.
  • Parallel current sources add; series voltage sources add; resistors combine as usual between swaps.
B16 · Practice Problem 4.6Source transformation practice
Question

Find io in the circuit of Fig. 4.19 using source transformation.

Try it first

Obtain vo in the circuit of Fig. 4.93 using source transformation. Check your result using PSpice or MultiSim.

C · Thevenin's and Norton's theorems (§4.5–4.6)

Source transformation (done)→Thevenin / Norton: Voc, Isc, Rth→Max power (next)

Where this sits. Part A, section B taught the method and its three Rth cases (switch off and combine; Voc/Isc or test source with dependent sources; test source only when there is no independent source). These are practice. Isc is always counted from a to b through the short, so Rth = Voc/Isc keeps its sign.

B45 · Problem 4.42Thevenin · challenging, floating terminals new idea
Question

For the circuit in Fig. 4.109, find the Thevenin equivalent between terminals a and b.

Hint: what's new
  • Merge parallel branches with sources first. Between M (above the 5 A) and b there are two branches: 20 Ω, and 20 Ω + 20 V. Together they are 10 Ω in series with 10 V (rising towards b). 5 A ∥ 10 Ω → 50 V behind 10 Ω.
  • Symmetry for Rth. With sources off: a–ground 10 Ω, a–M 10 Ω, M–ground 10 Ω, M–b 10 Ω, b–ground 10 Ω. Push 1 A in at a and out at b: by symmetry VM = 0 and Vb = −Va.

Voc. a carries current only to M, so Va = 30 + VM2; b has only 10 Ω to ground, so Vb = VM + 102. KCL at M:

30 − VM20 + 50 − VM10 = VM + 1020⇒4VM = 120⇒VM = 30 V,Va = 30 V,Vb = 20 V

Rth. KCL at a with VM = 0: Va10 + Va10 = 1 ⇒ Va = 5 V, Vb = −5 V ⇒ Rth = 10 Ω.

Answer

Vth = Va − Vb = 10 V, Rth = 10 Ω (even problem; full node solve agrees)

B61 · Problem 4.58Thevenin · current-source output new idea
Question

The network in Fig. 4.124 models a bipolar transistor common-emitter amplifier connected to a load. Find the Thevenin resistance seen by the load.

Hint: what's new
  • A current source alone at the output. The only thing connecting the load's top terminal to the rest of the circuit is the dependent source bib. A current source in series fixes the terminal current, so no voltage you apply can change it.

Switch off vs and push a test current It into the output terminal. It can only flow through the dependent source, so It = bib. KCL at the middle node with vs = 0 (ib = −V/R1): (1 + b)ib = V/R2 gives V = 0 and ib = 0, so It = 0 for any applied voltage.

Answer

Rth → ∞ (an ideal current-source output; even problem. The full solve with a test source is singular, as it must be.)

Both branches are 60 Ω, so the 8 A splits 4 A each: Va = 4 × 50 = 200 V, Vb = 4 × 40 = 160 V.

Vth = 40 V,Rth = (10 + 20) ∥ (50 + 40) = 22.5 Ω,IN = 4022.5 = 1.778 A
Answer

Vth = 40 V, Rth = 22.5 Ω, IN = 1.7778 A (= App. D)

B63 · Problem 4.60Thevenin + Norton · challenging practice
Question

For the circuit in Fig. 4.126, find the Thevenin and Norton equivalent circuits at terminals a-b.

Rth = [(4 + 6) via the middle] ∥ [5 via the bottom] = 10 ∥ 5 = 3.333 Ω(2 A and 3 A open, 18 V and 10 V shorted)

Voc (b = 0). The middle branch current i flows a → 18 V → 4 Ω (with the 3 A added in) → 6 Ω → b: 6i = VQ and (Va − 18) − VQ = 4(i + 3), so i = Va − 3010. KCL at a:

2 + Va − 3010 + Va − 105 = 0⇒3Va = 30
Answer

Vth = 10 V, Rth = 3.333 Ω, IN = 3 A (even problem; full node solve agrees)

B64 · Problem 4.61Thevenin + Norton · symmetry practice
Question

Obtain the Thevenin and Norton equivalent circuits at terminals a-b of the circuit in Fig. 4.127.

Voc. The circuit is left–right symmetric, so both top nodes sit at the same V and no current flows in the 2 Ω between them. KCL at a top node and at the middle node M (bottom of its 6 Ω at −12 V):

V − 122 + V − VM6 = 0 ⇒ VM = 4V − 36;2(VM − V)6 + VM + 126 = 0 ⇒ V = 9.6 V

Isc (a grounded): solving the left and middle nodes gives VTL = 4.8 V, VM = −2.4 V, so

Isc = 122 + 4.82 + −2.46 = 6 + 2.4 − 0.4 = 8 A,Rth = 9.68 = 1.2 Ω
Answer

Vth = 9.6 V, Rth = 1.2 Ω, IN = 8 A (= App. D)

B65 · Problem 4.62Thevenin · no independent source practice
Question

Find the Thevenin equivalent of the circuit in Fig. 4.128.

Vth = 0. Push 1 A into a (b grounded). With io = VM/20 and vo = Va − VM:

KCL at a:1 + 0.1io = vo10 ⇒ vo = 10 + io;KCL at M:1 = io + VM − 2vo40
1 = io + 18io − 2040⇒io = 6058 A,VM = 20.69 V,Va = VM + vo = 31.72 V
Answer

Vth = 0, Rth = 31.72 Ω (even problem; full node solve agrees)

B66 · Problem 4.63Norton · no independent source practice
Question

Find the Norton equivalent for the circuit in Fig. 4.129.

This is Part A's Problem 5.34 (A34): test source gives V = −103I.

Answer

B67 · Problem 4.64Thevenin · no independent source practice
Question

Obtain the Thevenin equivalent seen at terminals a-b of the circuit in Fig. 4.130.

Vth = 0. Push It into a; ix = VN/2 and the source is 10ix = 5VN:

It = VN2 + VN − 5VN4 = −VN2⇒VN = −2It,Va = VN + 1·It = −It
Answer

Vth = 0, Rth = −1 Ω (even problem; full node solve agrees)

B68 · Problem 4.65Thevenin · terminal equation practice
Question

For the circuit shown in Fig. 4.131, determine the relationship between Vo and Io.

Vth = 32 × 1216 = 24 V,Rth = 4 ∥ 12 + 2 = 5 Ω,Vo = Vth − RthIo

Vo = 24 − 5Io (= App. D)

D · Maximum power transfer (§4.8)

Thevenin / Norton (done)→Max power: RL = Rth, Pmax = Vth2/4Rth→Chapter 10 AC versions (later)

Where this sits. Part A, section C covered the theorem. Every problem below is: find Vth and Rth at the load's terminals, then RL = Rth. Each answer was also checked by sweeping the load resistance on the full circuit and finding the peak.

B69 · Practice Problem 4.13Max power · dependent source practice
Question

Determine the value of RL that will draw the maximum power from the rest of the circuit in Fig. 4.52. Calculate the maximum power.

Voc. No current in the 4 Ω, so Vth = VM; vx = 9 − VM:

9 − VM2 = VM − 3(9 − VM)⇒9VM = 63⇒Vth = 7 V

Isc.

9 − VM2 = VM − 3(9 − VM) + VM4⇒VM = 6.632 V,Isc = VM4 = 1.658 A
RL = Rth = 71.658 = 4.222 Ω,Pmax = 494 × 4.222 = 2.901 W
Answer

RL = 4.222 Ω, Pmax = 2.901 W (= book)

B70 · Problem 4.66Max power · R between two nodes practice
Question

Find the maximum power that can be delivered to the resistor R in the circuit of Fig. 4.132.

Rth = 2 ∥ (3 + 5) = 1.6 Ω(looking in across R, sources off)

Vth. With R removed, one loop current i through 3 Ω and 2 Ω; the 5 Ω carries i − 6:

20 = 3i + 2i − 10 + 5(i − 6)⇒i = 6 A⇒VB = 0,VA = 20 − 18 = 2 V
Answer

Pmax = 224 × 1.6 = 0.625 W (at R = 1.6 Ω; even problem, sweep agrees)

B71 · Problem 4.67Max power · bridge practice
Question

The variable resistor R in Fig. 4.133 is adjusted until it absorbs the maximum power from the circuit. (a) Calculate the value of R for maximum power. (b) Determine the maximum power absorbed by R.

The 40 V sits across the left and right corners. Shorted, those corners merge:

Rth = (80 ∥ 20) + (10 ∥ 90) = 16 + 9 = 25 Ω
Vtop − Vright = 40 × 20100 = 8 V,Vbottom − Vright = 40 × 90100 = 36 V,Vth = −28 V
Answer

(a) R = 25 Ω (b) Pmax = 282100 = 7.84 W (= App. D)

B72 · Problem 4.68Max power · the trap new idea
Question

Compute the value of R that results in maximum power transfer to the 10-Ω resistor in Fig. 4.134. Find the maximum power.

Hint: what's new
  • The theorem picks the load, not the source. Here the fixed element (10 Ω) is the load and R is part of the source side. Matching RL = Rth does not apply; instead ask how the 10 Ω's current changes as R grows.

Node above the 10 Ω: 12 − VR = V − 810 + V20. As R grows from 0, V falls from 12 V towards 5.33 V, so the 10 Ω current (V − 8)/10 falls from 0.4 A through zero to −0.267 A. Its magnitude is largest at R = 0:

R = 0:V = 12 V,i10 = 0.4 A,P = 0.42 × 10 = 1.6 W
Answer

R = 0 Ω, Pmax = 1.6 W (even problem; a sweep of R confirms)

B73 · Problem 4.69Max power · negative Rth new idea
Question

Find the maximum power transferred to resistor R in the circuit of Fig. 4.135.

Hint: what's new
  • Negative Rth. If Rth < 0, the load current Vth/(Rth + R) has no finite maximum: it blows up as R → |Rth|. That is the book's "∞ (theoretically)". A real circuit would leave its linear range first.
Isc:100 − vo10k = vo40k + vo22k⇒vo = 58.67 V,Isc = vo22k + 0.003vo = 0.1787 A
Voc = −243.6 V (two node equations),Rth = −243.60.1787 = −1363.6 Ω
Answer

P → ∞ as R → 1363.6 Ω (= App. D, "∞ (theoretically)")

B74 · Problem 4.70Max power · dependent source practice
Question

Determine the maximum power delivered to the variable resistor R shown in the circuit of Fig. 4.136.

Vth. With R removed, nothing flows in the 6 Ω, so Vx = 0 and the dependent source is off. Then the right 5 Ω carries nothing either: Vth = VA = 4 × 1520 = 3 V.

Rth (4 V shorted, test current It in at the top of R, out at the bottom). The 6 Ω carries It, so Vx = 6It and the source is 18It:

5 Ω carries It + 18It = 19It;A sits on 5 ∥ 15 = 3.75 Ω carrying It
V = 95It + 3.75It + 6It = 104.75It⇒Rth = 104.75 Ω
Answer

R = 104.75 Ω, Pmax = 324 × 104.75 = 21.5 mW (even problem; sweep agrees)

B75 · Problem 4.71Max power · amplifier model practice
Question

For the circuit in Fig. 4.137, what resistor connected across terminals a-b will absorb maximum power from the circuit? What is that power?

vo = 8 × 14 = 2 V,source = −120vo = −240 V (+ at the bottom)
Vth = −240 × 4050 = −192 V,Rth = 10k ∥ 40k = 8 kΩ,Pmax = 192232000

R = 8 kΩ, Pmax = 1.152 W (= App. D)

B76 · Problem 4.72Thevenin + max power practice
Question

(a) For the circuit in Fig. 4.138, obtain the Thevenin equivalent at terminals a-b. (b) Calculate the current in RL = 8 Ω. (c) Find RL for maximum power deliverable to RL. (d) Determine that maximum power.

Rth = 6 + (4 + 2) = 12 Ω

With a–b open, the 4 A sets the middle node at 4 × 2 = 8 V; the 2 A circulates through the 6 Ω, so Va = 8 + 12 = 20 V; b sits at −20 V.

Vth = 40 V,i8Ω = 4012 + 8 = 2 A,Pmax = 4024 × 12 = 33.33 W
Answer

(a) 40 V, 12 Ω (b) 2 A (c) RL = 12 Ω (d) 33.33 W (even problem; full solves agree)

B77 · Problem 4.73Max power · bridge practice

Determine the maximum power that can be delivered to the variable resistor R in the circuit of Fig. 4.139.

Vleft = 60 × 2030 = 40 V,Vright = 60 × 530 = 10 V,Vth = 30 V

B78 · Problem 4.74Max power · symbolic bridge practice
Question

For the bridge circuit shown in Fig. 4.140, find the load RL for maximum power transfer and the maximum power absorbed by the load.

With vs shorted the top and bottom rails merge:

RL = Rth = R1R2R1 + R2 + R3R4R3 + R4,Vth = vs(R2R1 + R2 − R4R3 + R4)
Answer

B79 · Problem 4.75Max power · design R practice
Question

For the circuit in Fig. 4.141, determine the value of R such that the maximum power delivered to the load is 3 mW.

Vth = 1 + 2 + 33 = 2 V,Rth = R3,Pmax = 44R/3 = 3R = 3 × 10−3
Answer

R = 1 kΩ (= App. D; the load is then RL = R/3 = 333.3 Ω)

Reading the figure

The wire from the top R crosses the middle R's wire with no dot. The book's answer (1 kΩ) requires all three R's to meet at the output node; if only the middle R reached it, R would be 333 Ω.
